title: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Perception and analysis are themselves carried out by simple programs

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The basic mechanisms underlying human perception and scientific analysis, like the mechanisms behind many natural processes, can be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 10: Processes of Perception and Analysis

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the evidence we have suggests that the basic mechanisms at work can once again successfully be captured by simple programs based on simple rules.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 10, “Processes of Perception and Analysis”; section “Introduction” (from p. 547), p. 547. Scope: human perception and methods of mathematical, statistical and computational analysis

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch10-01: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.47

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing benchmarks can test compact models on selected tasks. They cannot establish a single simple-program account across perception and scientific analysis, nor uniquely distinguish mechanism from approximation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Select defined perception and scientific-analysis tasks and compare compact rule-based programs with alternative models on behavioral accuracy and generalization, accounting for program description length. Broad success by compact programs supports restricted versions; systematic failures requiring task-specific complexity weaken them.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The scope spans heterogeneous perceptual and scientific activities.

'Basic mechanisms' and 'simple' are representation-dependent.

Behavioral fit does not identify neural mechanism.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.45
data adequacy: 0.38
data existence: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.42

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Many perceptual and analytic tasks already have simple algorithmic models, and public texture and neural datasets can test particular ones. The claim covers human perception and scientific analysis in general. Existing resources speak to examples, not to the assertion that the basic mechanisms as a class are captured by simple rules.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Take standard tasks in perception and in statistical or mathematical analysis and test whether a short rule-based program matches human or textbook performance on public stimuli. Success on a task supports the claim for that task; a basic perceptual or analytic capacity that remains unmatched by any simple program would limit the universal reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Matching a task with a short program does not show that the human mechanism is that program.

'Basic mechanisms' and 'simple rules' have no agreed size cutoff.
